newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: After Pyongyang's apology, a hard slog lies ahead.
newsitem.headline: After Pyongyang's apology, a hard slog lies ahead.

text.p: The apology, when it finally came, was made through clenched teeth -- two sentences on a crackling broadcast over Pyongyang radio.
And it was quickly drowned out by screeching anti-South Korean invective.
Still, it looks like North Korea got what it wanted from saying sorry for the first time over sneaking armed agents into the South aboard a submarine: food.
Its hungry, desperate people now have a better chance of surviving the harsh winter thanks to a deal Pyongyang struck with the United States.
Whether South Korea, the United States and their friends and neighbours get what they all yearn for -- a peace accord between the two Koreas on a nuclear-free peninsula -- is another matter.
It promises to be a hard slog. Ahead lie months, and probably years, of tortuous negotiations.
First, North Korea must be persuaded to get on speaking terms with the South.

That is no easy task considering that just this week Pyongyang was calling South Korean President Kim Young-sam a "ruthless tyrant". Besides, its goal is to bypass Seoul and sign a peace accord directly with Washington.
Many diplomats and North Korea analysts in Seoul believe Kim will have to leave office before dialogue can get out of the starting blocks. His single term expires in early 1988.
Separately, an international consortium supplying nuclear reactors to North Korea must extract guarantees on everything from free passage of its technicians to telephone links and safety standards.
A raft of protocols has to be worked out even before the first truckload of concrete is poured.
South Korea is supplying the light-water reactors in return for a promise made by Pyongyang to the United States to abandon its atomic weapons programme.
In all this, North Korea remains one of the most unpredictable nations, with a knack for doing just the wrong thing at the wrong time.

Days after launching an investment promotion drive in September -- and as it was pleading for more international aid -- Pyongyang sent a submarine packed with commandos on a blundering espionage mission to the South.
The result: food aid dried up and investors stayed away.
Just getting Pyongyang to agree to attend a briefing on proposed four-way peace talks with the United States, South Korea and China has been a battle.

It was won finally in New York by U.S. diplomats as part of their deal with North Korean envoys under which South Korea got an apology over the submarine, and North Korea received assurances over food aid.
A senior U.S. official, briefing reporters anonymously, said Washington had no immediate plans to provide more food to North Korea but might chip in to an international appeal.
The United Nations World Food Programme is expected to launch an official appeal shortly and the United States was expected to offer $6 million.
In addition, the United States was prepared to consider easing trade sanctions on North Korea to allow private firms to barter food.
Beyond questions about whether Pyongyang desires peace talks at all is a more basic concern: can it even afford to send representatives to staff them?

North Korea is so poor that diplomats believe it will insist the briefing on the talks is held in a country where it maintains a large embassy -- such as Malaysia -- so its negotiators will get free bed and board.
There are even doubts over whether the North's Stalinist state, propped up by handouts from China and the West, will be around for much longer to negotiate with.
